content:
The case is made by critics of Islam and by a small number of Muslims. The hadith, it says, were collected two centuries after the Prophet and include forgeries. The Quran calls itself complete and fully explained (6:38; 6:114). So a believer should follow the Quran alone and set the reports aside.[1]

The hadith scholars knew of forgery long before the critics did, and they built the tools that expose it. The real question is whether the Quran points beyond itself to the example of the Prophet. Six answers follow.

"Obey God and obey the Messenger" (4:59) names two objects of obedience. "Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God" (4:80). "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, leave it" (59:7).[2]

The Quran also gives the Prophet the work of explaining it. "We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may make clear (litubayyina) to people what was sent down to them" (16:44). It calls him the best example for anyone who hopes in God (33:21).[2]

The Quran commands the prayer many times. It gives neither the number of daily prayers nor how many units each prayer has. It commands zakat and gives no rates or thresholds.[3]

It says that God's count of months is twelve, four of them sacred (9:36), and it names only Ramadan (2:185). The Prophet's words "Pray as you have seen me pray" (Bukhari 631) show how the practice reached the community: by example, from the first day.[3]

Every Muslim community prays in the same basic pattern. That shared practice is itself a record of the Sunnah, passed on by people who did it together.

Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (died 820) wrote the Risala partly to answer people who doubted the reports. He argued that "the Wisdom", which the Quran pairs with "the Book" (2:129; 62:2), is the Sunnah of the Prophet.[4]

His Jima' al-'Ilm records debates with people who rejected reports altogether. The objection is old, and so is the reply.[4]

In British India, Ahl-e-Quran groups formed in Lahore and Amritsar in the early twentieth century, and a larger movement grew there after 1938. In Egypt, an article titled "Islam is the Quran alone" appeared in the journal al-Manar in 1906.[5]

These groups have not agreed among themselves on the number of prayers or how to perform them. One later leader of such a group went so far as to reject two verses of the Quran itself (9:128-129).[5]

That record supports the second answer above. Without the Prophet's example, the community cannot agree on the most basic act it is commanded to do.

Daniel Brown's study shows that modern rejection of hadith grew out of colonial-era arguments about reform. Aisha Musa traces how early Muslims argued over the standing of the reports as scripture.[6]

Neither study supports the claim that the community had no Sunnah until the collections were written. The collections gathered what was already taught and practised.

The hadith scholars said so first. The chains of narrators (isnād), the books that list fabricated reports (mawḍū'āt), and the grading of narrators exist because the scholars knew that forgery was real.[7]

The consistent position is critical acceptance: test each report, keep what passes, and drop what fails. Rejecting every report throws away the Prophet's example together with the forgeries.

The Quran sends its reader to the Prophet, and the community learned to pray from him. The related articles are why five prayers?, Schacht, isnads and the dating of hadith and Muhammad never wrote it down. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 6:38, 6:114.
  2. Quran 4:59, 4:80, 59:7, 16:44, 33:21, 3:31.
  3. Quran 9:36, 2:185; Sahih al-Bukhari 631; the hadith texts are on searchtruth.com.
  4. Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i, The Epistle on Legal Theory (al-Risala), trans. Joseph E. Lowry (New York: NYU Press, 2013); Joseph E. Lowry, Early Islamic Legal Theory: The Risala of Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (Leiden: Brill, 2007).
  5. Daniel W. Brown, Rethinking Tradition in Modern Islamic Thought (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996), chapters 2 and 3.
  6. Brown, Rethinking Tradition; Aisha Y. Musa, Hadith as Scripture: Discussions on the Authority of Prophetic Traditions in Islam (New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008).
  7. Jonathan A. C. Brown, Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World (Oxford: Oneworld, 2009), chapters 3 and 9.
